statements.context: WASHINGTON, DC – US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Director Scott Kupor joined The Lead with Jake Tapper on CNN to discuss President Trump’s Super Intelligence Force, the administration’s approach to SI safety and innovation, and how the government can prepare for potential risks and workforce changes. WATCH HERE On President Trump’s use of the term “super intelligence”: “No. Yes. I can’t protect you, you know. But yes, SI is the new word.” On whether companies will change their names: “I don’t know. But you may have seen Elon did, right? So Elon changed the name of his company. He’s now calling it X SI, I believe.” On whether there will be punishment for using the term “artificial intelligence”: “I don’t know. You got to ask the President that. I’m not briefed on that to talk to you about today.” On the industry’s voluntary safety commitments and the task force’s role: “Yes. I would say a couple of things. First of all, it’s not just, you know, they’re responsible for their own stuff. As part of that contract they signed, they agreed that they would have external third-party auditors reviewing it. And as you probably know, obviously, if you sit on a public company board in particular, outside auditors typically report to the board of directors. “And so if an outside security auditor comes back to these companies and says, ‘Hey, we got a problem here,’ that board’s going to have to actually respond and do something. So it is truly legally binding in that respect, which is all the traditional fiduciary duties and kind of duties that board owes. “The second thing I would just add is, look, as I know we’ll talk about, the President put together this SI force that myself and three others—” “Jay Clayton, Emil Michael, and Andrew Ferguson at the FTC are running. I think you should expect that. Look, we’re not going to sit around and just say, ‘Great, we’re wonderful. We’re thrilled you guys signed this piece of paper,’ and, you know, we should just be done and dusted. “The whole purpose of this committee is to figure out, OK, what is the comprehensive set of policies that we think meet the dual goals that the President has?

statements.context: WASHINGTON, DC – US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Director Scott Kupor, Vice Chair of the Super Intelligence Task Force, joined CNBC’s Squawk Box to discuss the task force’s work, technology companies’ responsibilities, government oversight, the impact of data centers, and the need to advance super intelligence responsibly. WATCH HERE On the task force’s goals: “Thanks, Joe. You’re exactly right. The goal is to make sure that we continue to win, which we are winning, and ensure that we do so responsibly. I think what you’re going to see from us are a couple things. One is—and I just saw the last segment you guys did—there’s a lot of work on behalf of the industry that needs to happen.” On industry responsibility: “We’ve been very clear from the beginning, and you’ll see us continue to follow up. The industry bears a lot of responsibility here to make sure that when they release things, they’re safe, they’re appropriately vetted, and when things go wrong, you’re going to see us make sure that there’s a very appropriate ongoing notification program so that the government has all the information they need.” “We’re also going to make sure that all the major players outside of technology—critical infrastructure, financial services, energy, oil and gas, all these companies—have the appropriate information they need to make sure that they’ve got plans in place and that we’ve got coordination across things.” “There’s a whole set of laws that the President has mentioned—product liability laws, principal-agent laws, all these things that really govern corporate responsibility in these areas. I think you’re going to see a much greater articulation of that and an indication among the companies that the government has a very clear expectation of their responsibility here.” On enforcement and oversight: “You’re right. That was with a pact that was signed, I guess, a week ago Tuesday with the various players. These are independent auditors. They will report to the board, and all the traditional fiduciary duties and corporate responsibilities will attach to that.”
